opus-5.5.text:
I think a few things came together at roughly the same time, and that convergence is what makes this year feel different.

The first is that the base models finally got good enough at reasoning. Over the past year or so, we've seen that if you train a model with reinforcement learning to think before it answers, to work through a problem step by step, check itself, and backtrack when it's wrong, its capabilities jump in a very real way. Once a model can reason reliably over long horizons, you can trust it with something more than a single question-and-answer exchange. You can give it a task.

The second is that the industry's focus has shifted from "chat" to "doing." A chatbot answers you. An agent takes actions: it searches, writes and runs code, operates a browser, calls tools, and keeps going for many steps until the job is done. Products like deep research tools and coding agents showed people, for the first time, what it feels like when an AI goes off and works for you for ten or twenty minutes and comes back with something genuinely useful. That changed people's expectations almost overnight.

The third, which is closest to my own work, is that reinforcement learning has become the key technique for building agents. Pretraining gives you knowledge and imitation gives you a reasonable starting point, but to make an agent robust in a messy, multi-step environment, you need it to learn from its own trial and error. The bottleneck is no longer just data. It's the environment, the reward, and the RL infrastructure that lets you run huge numbers of long, asynchronous rollouts efficiently. That's a hard systems problem, and a lot of progress has happened there recently.

So when I say 2025 is the year of agents, I don't mean agents are solved. They still make silly mistakes, and long-horizon reliability is far from where it needs to be. What I mean is that this is the year the paradigm became clear. People now broadly agree that the next big leap comes from agents trained with RL to interact with the real world, and both the technology and the products have reached the point where you can actually see that future taking shape.

r002.rationale: It does not identify a shift from text-only to multimodal reasoning.

r003.rationale: It contrasts chatbots that answer with agents that take actions through tools and continue for many steps, and describes agents learning through trial and error in environments.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd say the honest answer is that 2025 wasn't the year agents suddenly worked because of some brand-new idea. It was the year a few things that had been building separately finally lined up.

The first is the models themselves. Through 2023 and most of 2024, if you asked a model to do a ten-step task, the failure probability compounded. Even a 95 percent success rate per step gives you a coin flip after about fifteen steps. That's why early agent demos looked amazing in a video and fell apart when you actually used them. What changed with the reasoning-focused models and with reinforcement learning on long-horizon tasks is that per-step reliability climbed enough, and the models got better at noticing their own mistakes and backing up. Recovery matters more than never failing. Once a model can realize "that didn't work, let me try something else," the compounding math stops killing you.

The second is that the environment side matured. Coding was the first real agent domain, and not by accident. Code gives you a verifiable signal: the tests pass or they don't, the program compiles or it doesn't. That lets you do RL at scale with real rewards instead of human preference labels. So you saw coding agents go from autocomplete to actually finishing tasks on their own, and that became the template. People in the industry started asking: what else has a checkable outcome? Browsing, data analysis, some scientific workflows. Those followed.

The third thing is infrastructure, which sounds boring but is what made it a "year" rather than a research result. Tool-use protocols, standardized ways to give a model access to files, browsers, APIs, memory across sessions. In 2024 every team was hand-wiring this. By 2025 it was becoming plumbing you could just assume.

And I'd add one more that's more about my own background. I spent years in multi-agent RL, and the lesson there was that a single agent's capability ceiling is set by the environment it trains in. For a long time language models trained on static text, so they were great at talking and weak at doing. Agents are what you get when the training environment itself becomes interactive. So from where I sit, 2025 is less a product trend and more the point where the training paradigm shifted from imitation toward interaction. That's the deeper reason I call it the year of agents. Not that the products are finished, they clearly aren't, but the flywheel started turning.

r001.rationale: The response says agent products are not finished and frames 2025 as a training-paradigm shift, but it does not state that commercial maturity will lag the capability breakthroughs visible in 2025.

r002.rationale: The response discusses reasoning-focused models and interactive training, but it does not identify a shift from text-only to multimodal reasoning.

r003.rationale: The response describes agents interacting with their environment, recognizing failures, trying alternatives, and using tools to complete tasks—communicating a move from one-shot responses to closed-loop interaction.

astra-6.text:
I think 2025 marks a shift from AI that answers questions to AI that can carry out tasks. With a chatbot, you ask a question, get a response, and then do the work yourself. With an agent, you give it a goal, and it can take steps toward that goal—use tools, look at the results, and adjust what it does next.

That requires several capabilities to come together: reasoning, tool use, and the ability to follow a task over multiple steps. As those capabilities improve, it becomes possible to delegate useful pieces of work, even if a person still needs to supervise.

So when I say “the year of AI agents,” I don’t mean that everything suddenly becomes autonomous or that reliability is solved. I mean that the focus shifts toward getting work done. The important question becomes: can this system complete a real task reliably enough that you would choose to delegate it?

r002.rationale: It discusses reasoning and tool use but does not identify a shift from text-only to multimodal reasoning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think 2025 is the year when AI starts moving from answering questions to carrying out tasks. A chatbot can tell you how to do something; an agent can take a goal, use tools, observe what happens, and adjust its next step.

What makes that shift possible is the combination of stronger reasoning, better tool use, and the ability to work through longer sequences of actions. That opens up useful applications in coding, research, and everyday workflows.

But I wouldn’t say that means fully autonomous agents are suddenly ready for everything. Reliability is still the key challenge. If an agent makes a mistake halfway through a task, can it recognize that, recover, or ask a person for help? My expectation is that the first real successes will come in well-defined tasks where results can be checked. So, for me, “the year of agents” means the beginning of practical adoption, with humans still providing direction and oversight.

r001.rationale: It describes practical adoption beginning in 2025 but does not say commercial maturity will lag the year's capability breakthroughs.
